did_you_know.text: In this chapter, contact with a dead body creates a temporary ritual status, not necessarily a moral sin. Priests had to avoid it so they could continue serving in the sanctuary.
Shaving the head, cutting the beard, and scratching the skin were mourning customs known in the ancient world. The Torah forbids them to priests to emphasize their special status.
The phrase “filled his hand” is not about literally filling a hand; it is an ancient expression for appointing someone to a sacred office.
The word nezer can mean both “crown” and “consecration.” Here it connects the anointing oil on the high priest’s head with his special status.
The chapter distinguishes between belonging to the priestly family and being eligible for certain sanctuary duties. A physical condition affects the ritual role, but does not erase family membership.
The exact meaning of several medical terms in this list is uncertain, so translations sometimes differ. This reminds us that ancient texts do not always use medical terms as we do today.
A priest who could not serve at the altar was still allowed to eat sacred food. This shows the difference between being restricted from a duty and losing priestly status.
At the end of the chapter, Moses speaks not only to Aaron and his sons but also to all the Israelites. This emphasizes that priestly rules were a public matter for the whole community to know.
